extraction.name: COMMONSENSEQA
extraction.description: A dataset for commonsense question answering built from ConceptNet relations, where crowd-workers author multiple-choice questions that distinguish between target concepts sharing the same relation to a source concept. It contains 12,247 questions.
extraction.creator: Alon Talmor; Jonathan Herzig; Nicholas Lourie; Jonathan Berant
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created by extracting subgraphs from ConceptNet and then using crowd-workers to author and filter multiple-choice commonsense questions, with additional distractors added and relevant snippets collected via a search engine.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw/source data consisted of knowledge extracted from ConceptNet subgraphs, with one source concept and three target concepts sharing a semantic relation.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowdworkers authored multiple-choice questions based on ConceptNet subgraphs, were instructed to create questions with high language variation, crowdworkers filtered questions by quality, and crowdworkers added distractors.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper analyzes annotation outputs by examining language variation in authored questions and manually annotating a random sample of 100 development examples for commonsense skill types, allowing multiple skills per question.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: One authored multiple-choice question per extracted subgraph, with multiple distractors added to form answer choices.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: 122 question formulators contributed; 10 workers formulated more than 85% of the questions.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for commonsense question answering research, including training and evaluating models on questions that require prior knowledge rather than only provided context.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Post-preprocessing dataset construction included grouping ConceptNet triplets into question sets, adding two additional distractors per question, filtering questions by human verification, and augmenting each question with retrieved web snippets as textual context.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: ConceptNet was filtered before dataset creation: removed triplets with overly general or already well-explored relations, removed triplets with concepts longer than four words or not in English, and removed triplets whose two concepts had very low edit distance.

name.evidence: we present COMMONSENSEQA: a challenging new dataset for commonsense question answering.

description.evidence: we present COMMONSENSEQA: a challenging new dataset for commonsense question answering. To capture common sense beyond associations, we extract from CONCEPTNET ... multiple target concepts that have the same semantic relation to a single source concept. Crowd-workers are asked to author multiple-choice questions... We create 12,247 questions through this procedure

creator.evidence: Alon Talmor ... Jonathan Herzig ... Nicholas Lourie Jonathan Berant

inLanguage.evidence: Where on a river can you hold a cup upright to catch water on a sunny day?

rai:dataCollection.evidence: “We generate multiple-choice questions in a process that comprises the following steps. 1. We extract subgraphs from CONCEPTNET, each with one source concept and three target concepts.”

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: “Crowd-workers are asked to author multiple-choice questions”

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: “To capture common sense beyond associations, we extract from CONCEPTNET (Speer et al., 2017) multiple target concepts that have the same semantic relation to a single source concept.”

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: “Crowd-workers are asked to author multiple-choice questions that mention the source concept and discriminate in turn between each of the target concepts.”; “Question formulators were instructed to create questions with high language variation.”; “Crowdworkers filter questions by quality”; “Crowdworkers add distractors”

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: “We analyzed the distribution of first and second words in the formulated questions along with example questions.”; “we randomly sampled 100 examples from the development set and performed the following analysis. For each question, we explicitly annotated the types of commonsense skills that a human uses to answer the question. We allow multiple commonsense skills per questions”

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: “We extract subgraphs from CONCEPTNET, each with one source concept and three target concepts.”; “Crowd-workers are asked to author multiple-choice questions”; “Crowdworkers add distractors”

rai:annotatorDemographics.evidence: “122 formulators contributed to question generation. However, 10 workers formulated more than 85% of the questions.”

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: “we present COMMONSENSEQA: a challenging new dataset for commonsense question answering” and “Our best baseline is based on BERT-large ... and obtains 56% accuracy, well below human performance”

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: “for each question concept q and relation r we group three different triplets” ; “we ask crowd-workers to add two additional incorrect answers to each formulated question” ; “only questions verified by at least one worker that answered correctly are used. This processes filters out 15% of the questions.” ; “We take the first 100 result snippets for each of the five answer candidates, yielding a context of 500 snippets per question.”

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: “We filter triplets with general relations (e.g., RelatedTo) or relations that are already well-explored in NLP (e.g., IsA).” ; “We filter triplets where one of the concepts is more than four words or not in English.” ; “We filter triplets where the edit distance between c1 and c2 is too low.”
